title: Cache-Aware Joint Router Adaptation for Memory-Efficient MoE Inference (Zhenhe Wu, Yaping Jin, Qinghua Xing, Hang Zhou, Wei He, Xianjie Wu, Xianfu Cheng, Jian Yang, Hanting Chen; Huawei / Beihang / others; arXiv v2, 10 Sep 2026)
setup: Models: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (48 layers, ~30.5B total / 3.3B active, 128 experts/layer, top-8) and GPT-OSS-20B (24 layers, ~21B / 3.6B, 32 experts/layer, top-4) -- NOTE the paper uses GPT-OSS-20B, not 120B. Hardware: 8-accelerator node, 140 GB device memory each (training/eval); no latency measured at all. Metrics come from a trace-driven simulator synchronised with greedy decoding (hit rate, load-adjusted hit, MB of expert traffic per decode token; prefill transfers excluded). Cache: B=20 of 128 experts per layer for Qwen3 (15.6 %), B=8 of 32 for GPT-OSS (25 %). Batch 1 per device. Tasks GSM8K, MATH, CommonsenseQA (validation). Baselines: LRU/LFU/LRFU run on matched LM-only post-trained backbones; prefetchers Least-Stale (SpecMD), ProMoE, FineMoE, Temporally-Extended MoE. Method needs 4 epochs of post-training of the backbone plus auxiliary routers (12.6M extra params for Temporal Router on Qwen3, 25.2M for full mode).

why: Needs post-training of the model (retraining required), so it cannot apply to a fixed 125B checkpoint; no latency measured (simulator MB/token); cache is 15.6 % of experts per layer (about 2.5 footprints on a top-8/128 model), the same order as our 8-32 GB cases but only simulated; GPU-class host, batch 1 per device. The idea (learn same-layer retention so the same experts recur) is the 'router fine-tuned for temporal stickiness' family, and it reports the price: concentration of expert use (top-8 mass 36.8 -> 48.6 % at sw 0.1->2.0).

ablation: Yes: auxiliary-only (frozen backbone) vs joint (Table 2): hit 63.01 vs 73.13; temporal-only vs spatio-only vs full; B and R sweeps (Table 3); sw sweep. Isolates the benefit of changing the model itself (+10 points hit over a frozen model with learned retention).
limitations: Stated: metrics are coverage/traffic not latency; each B uses a separate checkpoint (effects include model adaptation); baselines are different complete configurations rather than policies on an identical trace (Sect. 4.1); GPT-OSS results mixed/task dependent.
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction. Consistent with the idea that gains need model change; its LRU hit of ~61 % at 15.6 % cache on Qwen3 is in the range of our LRU numbers on the same model family (our 0.56 at 2.1 footprints = 13 % of pairs, B.md s1 #8).

why: GPU (A100) emulation, 5 GB/s link, models with 8-64 experts, TTFT-dominated metrics, cache measured as share of ALL experts with a prefetcher. The one insight that transfers is the cyclic-scan pathology: with a cache below ~1 footprint a plain LRU thrashes inside a single forward pass (collision misses); Least-Stale protects the current pass. Our own LRU at 0.96 footprints is exactly 0.000 (B.md s1 #10), so a published eviction fix exists for the regime where we found a pin helpful (inference, not tested).
quality_loss: Not for the headline Least-Stale (lossless eviction). Lossy options: Drop priority -5..-30 %, Substitution score 'fails across all configurations' (GSM8K 0.073 / 0.037 / 0.027 / 0.008, Table 1 Config2), cache-aware routing lambda 0.1-0.5 trade-off.
ablation: Yes: eviction x prefetch x miss-handling x routing grid (Fig. 4-9, Table 1-2); Least-Stale as drop-in on four prior systems.
limitations: Authors: 100 samples/task; emulated hardware; 'Configurations selected perform well in most cases but this is not the point' (platform paper); Least-Stale not helpful for all (Phi-3.5 + Zhu'25).
contradicts_our_findings: Partly: abstract says expert access 'is not consistent with temporal locality (LRU, LFU)'; we measured LRU > pin at >=10 % share across decode tokens (B.md s1 #10), i.e. temporal locality exists across tokens. The two are reconcilable: SpecMD's complaint is within-pass layer-order thrash at tiny capacity (1-5 % of all experts, below one footprint), which is the cliff in our LRU row (0.000 at 0.96 fp).

title: Which Expert Misses Are Worth Waiting For? Substitution and Caching for Mixture-of-Experts Inference on a Consumer GPU (ChaeWoo Son, independent researcher; Research Square preprint v1, not peer reviewed; DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-11268552/v1)

why: Same expert geometry as our target (512 experts, top-10, 48 layers, ~Q4 GGUF 48.5 GB) and the first paper in this batch with batch-1 llama.cpp numbers and NVMe reads (5.7 GB/s O_DIRECT). But: (1) attention and the resident 25 % expert cache are on an RTX 3090 (15.7 GiB VRAM) and stock baseline also has GPU; in our CPU-only regime the baseline is a CPU run, and the 'miss' cost is a disk read of an expert (1.9 MB for the Q4_K_M expert) followed by CPU compute, not a PCIe copy; (2) the cache is 25 % of experts in VRAM (we have about 2-8 token footprints of expert RAM, i.e. a few percent of the 24.6k expert slices of the 125B); (3) substitution is lossy (+1.2-1.8 % ppl, up to -1.8 GSM8K points for the 0.15 rule alone, -8.4 at 12.5 % cache); (4) teacher forcing with ample page cache confounds. What does transfer: the quality side of substituting misses, measured on a 512-expert top-10 model: only about 7.5 % of expert calls are substituted at 25 % cache and mass (summed gate weight of substituted experts) 0.056-0.21 depending on test; gate-weight threshold is a usable quality guard for cache-aware routing in our family.
quality_loss: Teacher-forced ppl +0.35 % (idealised emulation) / +1.21 % (engine, 0.15 rule) / +0.67 % (quality-first policy) at 25 % cache; 12.5 % cache first-choice rule +3.61 %; generation accuracy GSM8K -1.8 points (0.15 rule alone, CI touches 0), +0.4 / -0.2 for Q / S; HumanEval within -2.44..+0.61. Mass correlates with ppl (0.77 on 6, 0.92 on 24 sessions).
ablation: Yes: substitute-all vs first-choice vs 0.15 rule (Table 2/3); frequency eviction, background admission (beta 0.5), per-layer slot allocation (Sect. 6.1); SSD-only vs page-cache-first read path (Table 8); RAM conditions. Cache vs layout vs prefetch is NOT isolated; they state they did not compare with prefetching or lower-precision copies.
limitations: Stated: one model, mostly 25 % cache; quality mainly teacher-forced ppl; only the generation test and Experiment B were pre-planned; two conclusions reversed when the sample grew 6 -> 24; speed differs 24-41 % across hosts; one machine for the stock comparison; baseline is a single stock config; RAM conditions artificial; no comparison to prefetching or KTransformers/Fiddler; Experiment B reached no judgment; the page-cache-first gain may come from the engine's own loading.
contradicts_our_findings: No. It supports our family s1 #8 claim that substituting heavy misses costs quality and that gains need a threshold; but it contradicts our assumption that cache-aware routing must change ~12-42 % of the router's choices (our B.md: LRU 0.56 -> 0.79 changes 24 %): here only 7.5 % of calls are substituted at 25 % cache, and fetching the heavy ones keeps ppl near +1 %. That suggests a gate-weight-guarded bias (fetch if first choice or weight >= 0.15) is a cheaper quality guard than the plain top-k swap we modelled.

ablation: Yes (Sect. 6.3): CGOPipe vs not; HRM-found policy vs fixed; bottleneck analysis. Not cache vs layout vs prefetch.
limitations: Authors note variable prompt length and padding variants, throughput-oriented only; attention on CPU becomes bottleneck at long prompts/generation lengths.

Datasets LMSYS-Chat-1M and ShareGPT; mean input 37/43 and output 127/122 tokens; 64 prompts averaged; batch 1 for the main figure, batch 1-8 sensitivity. Experts in host DRAM; the system stores 'expert maps' + semantic embeddings of earlier prompts and uses them to guide prefetch distance d=3.

why: Experts in 128 GB host RAM over PCIe 4.0; GPU computes experts; no NVMe; models 16-57B with 64-ish experts; the key win comes from overlapping PCIe with GPU compute, which does not exist for CPU compute reading from disk. Authors themselves note that CPU compute (LO) wins at low cache rates and for Mixtral. In decode the gain over LRU is 1.31x, mostly because misses are hidden; hit rate unchanged.
ablation: Yes (Fig. 12, 13): prefetch, chunked prefetch, early preemption, reordered inference; cache-rate sweep (Fig. 14-16); batch and model size sweeps.
limitations: Authors: prefetching alone does not help prefill (all experts needed); LO beats cache systems at low cache rates in decode; llama.cpp gains smaller due to faster compute.
contradicts_our_findings: No. Supports that static caches lose to LRU in decode (their: LRU beats static in decode, 'some reuse of experts across iterations'), matching our pin < LRU.
